label: text
text: THE MANY PAY.

label: text
text: (Reutor's Service.)

label: text
text: London, May

label: text
text: Mr. Winston Churchill, in a speech at the Primrose League meeting in the Albert Hall, said the Budget consisted of a series of carefully adjusted balances.

label: text
text: The tax on silk would produce exactly £4,000,000 this year and £7,000,000 next year which would precisely meet the cost of the relief given on the earned incomes of smaller taxpayers.

label: text
text: He was confident that the silk tax would not diminish employment. It would be paid by an enormous number of people in inconceivably small instalments. The women, if they were convinced it was for the country's good, would not hesitate to assume the burden of the tax.

label: text
text: 300W MUGCH. London, May 11.

label: text
text: In reply to enquiries whether it was intended to charge the full ad valorem duty of $33.1/3 per cent. in the case of imported made up goods of which silk is relatively a small component, the Treasury explains that the point was carefully considered when the duties were framed.

label: text
text: The desirability of modifying the charge in such cases is appreciated. Accordingly steps are being taken to consult the interests concerned with a view to a satisfactory solution regarding the method to be employed.

label: text

IMPORTANT SUBERIAN
CONCESSION.

label: text
text: Representatives of the Soviets and the Lena Goldfields Co. have signed a draft agreement for concessionary exploitation by the company, to be called the Lena Gold Enterprises, of 1,500,000 acres of gold, silver, copper and lead bearing areas in the Lena, Altai and Sissersk regions of Siberia.

label: text
text: It is understood that important New York banking and mining interests have considerable participation in the operations of the company which embraces the interests of a number of companies which before the var operated the mines covered by the present concession under concession.

label: text
text: The Soviet will turn over to the company river craft for transport on the Lena River. Six per cent. of the total production is payable to the Soviet. The company's technical staff will be largely British and American.

label: paragraph_title
text: BACK TO GOLD.

label: text
text: (Reuter's American Service.)

label: text
text: The Secretary of Commerce, Mr. Hoover, has issued a statement to the effect that with the return of the pound to a gold basis the entire international trade will be calculated in terms of gold prices. He predicts that, with a general condition of stability prices will be reached which should be reduced to the benefit of commerce and industry all over the world.

label: text
text: He added that the German mark prices will now be absolutely on a gold base, the Dawes plan having linked up the German coinage to a degree with the pound sterling. It is very certain that the effect of the English move will be to reduce the volume of speculative hazard in international trade, because of the elimination of risks that must be taken with currency of fluctuating value. There will probably be a small swing of prices in Britain as the adjustment is made, but the gain in stability will bring benefits likely to outweigh any losses.

label: paragraph_title
text: The Value of Old Alliances..

label: text
text: THE PATH OF AMITY.

label: text
text: HOW THE NATIONS MUST CO-OPERATE:

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: Mr. Winston Churchill, in his speech at the Primrose League meeting, referring to foreign policy, said that world peace depended on faithful co-operation between the two groups of the greatest nations of today.

label: text
text: In the new world the Washington Agreement had woven together British, the United States and Japan in a bond of friendship and anity which should preserve the peace and freedom of the seas for many generations.

label: text
text: In the old world we were endeavouring to establish a British French Italian and German security pack.

label: text
text: Just us the Washington Agreement was not reached by casting inside the old and valued alliance with Japan but by merging it in a larger grouping with the United States, so our policy in Europe would not develop by casting inside trusted allies by whom we stood in the dark days of the war.

label: paragraph_title
text: HOURS OF WORK.

label: paragraph_title
text:
INTERNATIONAL ACTION
NEEDED

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: London, May

label: text
text: The House of Commons by 223 to 128 votes rejected a motion by Mr. G. Buchanan (Labour) for the second reading of a private member's Bill based on the Washington eight hours convention providing that the hours of labour in industrial occupations, except of seamen and farm labourers, should not exceed 48 a week.

label: text
text: Mr. D. Kirkwood (Labour), in seconding the Bill, vigorously protested against the efforts of the engineering employers to increase the hours of labour.

label: text
text: Mr. R. G. Clarry (Conservative), in moving the rejection of the Bill declared it would injure industry and increase unemployment. The provisions of the Washington Convention could only be effectively introduced by simultaneous legislative action in all the countries whose representatives signed the Convention.

label: text
text: Sir Arthur Steel Maitland, Minister of Labour, expressed his willingness if necessary to consult the representatives of other countries in regard to securing the aim of the Convention.

label: paragraph_title
text: PRINCE IN AFRICA

label: text
text: (Reuter's Serolne.)

label: text
text: After a dance at the Government House last night, attended by several hundred guests, at which the Prince of Wales danced un-tiringly, the Prince was out at 9:30 this morning. His appearance occasioned a most successful unrehearsed demonstration—bands of massed students including hundreds of attractive girls in university gowns outside the Government House, a body of comic cavalry armed with brooms and brushes followed by an ox-waggond draped in blue and white and drawn by twelve oxen. The immense procession of cheering and laughing students sang in chorus a specially written song, urging the Prince of Wales not to be "down in the mouth."

label: text
text: The Prince was very amused and seated himself on the waggon and drove the oxen which led the procession through the city, while he accompanied the whole-hearted crowd singing "he's a jolly good fellow" to the crowded city hall, where the Prince of Wales was ceremoniously installed as chancellor of the University of Capetown, which he has occupied since the inauguration of the university in 1918, and given the honorary degree of Laws.

label: text
text: The proceedings were marked with good-humoured ragging, including the appearance on the platform of a little white hen wearing the varsity football colours, also a parade round the hall, a counterfeit presentment of Mr. Ramsay MacDonald and the singing songs addressed to the Prince of Wales as "dear old Ted."—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: DO HIGHLY-PAID JOBS GO BEGGING?

label: text
text: LONDON CONTROVERSY

label: paragraph_title
text: Talented Youth Said To Be Unrecognised.

label: text
text: Are young men in business worth £10,000 a year? If so, are the men available, or is it the position that is lacking?

label: text
text: An interesting controversy along these lines is in progress among the heads of big London business firms, initiated by the managing director of Whiteley's, London's huge emporium, who says the jobs are awaiting suitable men, if they can be found. To this the rejoinder is made that the talent in young men is frequently not recognised, and that in this way some of the elderly leaders of commerce prove their own unworthiness for the large salaries they are drawing.

label: text
text: According to Mr. John Lawrie,

label: paragraph_title
text: R. A. A CONCERT

label: text
text: "LAST NIGHTS GREAT SUCCESS."

label: text
text: Well arranged, with excellently chosen items rendered very capably by good artists, the concert at the Tleatre Royal in aid of the funds of the R.A.A. could only be found fault with in one respect and that was in regard to the length of the programme.

label: text
text: The East Surreys Band delighted with their rendering of Sullivan's "Imperial" and a selection from Ponchielli's "La Gioconda".

label: text
text: The place of Mrs. R. Mathieson, who was unable to be present, was taken by Mrs. O. C. Womack who pleased the audience greatly with "Friend Of Mine," "Oh No, John" and "I Built A Fairy Palace," and the charming voice of the other lady vocalist (Mrs. S. Collett) was well suited to Cowen's "May Song" and Montague Phillip's "Sing Joyous Bird."

label: text
text: Mr. Bert Burfows was the "hit" of the evening in so far as carrying the greater part of the audience with him was concerned. His appeal lies in the very natural manner in which he conveys impressions and expressions and whether it was in patter with Miss Gladys Brock or with the assistance of three little ladies tripping about the stage (Misses Irene Deacon, Doreen Smith and Audrey Steel) he had his audience following his every movement.

label: text
text: In spite of the fact that his confrere, Mr. Stilas, was unable to take part, Mr. Zellensky captivated the audience with impromptu characterisations which appealed to all. Perhaps the most successful character acting, although of an entirely different nature to Mr. Zellensky's, however, was that of Mr. Chas. O'Ive who amongst other things gave Mathias's dream and a Dickensian sketch.

label: text
text: Clever in composition and execution was the “Old Fashioned Drama,” given by Major Macready and Mrs. F. C. Hall. Major Macready later gave a humorous song, whilst Mr. H. E. Gardner rendered “Awake” and “Love is Mine,” most acceptably.

label: text
text: "The Daily Sketch," which interviewed heads of big firms, finds these jobs are will-o-the-wisps. Youth, knocking at the gate and anxious for a chance to show the stuff of which he is made, is unable to find an outlet for his energies.

label: text
text: Sir Herbert Morgan, chairman of MacFisheries, declares that there would be plenty of talented young men available if given scope and opportunity. Some elderly leaders of commerce would have got nowhere if they had had to begin in these days of keener competition.

label: text
text: "If they can't find men capable of filling big posts," he said, "they are deficient in judgment and initiative and unworthy of the huge salaries they are drawing. It is useless for the head of a big business to sit in his chair and lament that he can't find young men worthy of holding £10,000 jobs. Does he expect them to stop from the skies? If they did, I do not expect he would recognise them. It is the duty of the heads of big businesses to attract young men of marked capacity. They ought to possess the instinct for spotting talent."

label: text
text: Mr. W. Reith, managing director of the British Broadcasting Co., Ltd., says that older business men often regard able youngsters with suspicion. A common fault in big businesses is the placing of young men in watertight compartments, instead of giving them an opportunity for all-round experience.

label: text
text: Sir Edward. Manville, vice-chairman of the Federation of British Industries, said: "There is only a limited number of highly-paid posts and I am not aware of any £10,000 job which is vacant. I know of an industry that would be willing to pay £20,000 a year to the right man. It is not the question of a vacancy, but of the opportunity to create a post worth the salary. Employers would not risk appointing to such a post a man with insufficient experience."
